statement: Tlacaelel, who held the cihuacoatl office (chief counselor/co-ruler) under several successive Mexica tlatoque across roughly six decades (d. 1487), is credited by multiple sources with reorganizing Mexica state theology in the mid-15th century, elevating Huitzilopochtli from a comparatively minor tribal/patron deity to co-equal imperial-patron status with the established regional gods Tlaloc, Tezcatlipoca, and Quetzalcoatl, and recasting Mexica identity as a "chosen people" obligated to feed the sun through war-captive sacrifice. He is also credited, with lower confidence, with ordering the burning of earlier historical codices to erase rival/humbler origin accounts — a claim repeated across secondary/tertiary sources but not traced to a strong primary-source citation in this research pass. Huitzilopochtli's birth myth (the Coatepec narrative) is textually attested only in Sahagún's post-conquest Florentine Codex, Book 3 (1575-1577); the Coyolxauhqui monolith (Templo Mayor excavations) provides independent pre-conquest archaeological corroboration of the myth's antiquity in sculptural form, even though no pre-conquest text survives.

sources.citation: General secondary/tertiary sourcing on Tlacaelel's theological reforms (Grokipedia "Tlacaelel"; Wikipedia "Cihuacoatl (position)"), cross-checked against Templo Mayor archaeological reporting on the Coyolxauhqui monolith.

notes: The Tlacaelel book-burning claim specifically should be treated as moderate-confidence, not certain, per the research agent's own flag — it was not traced to a strong primary-source citation (e.g. a full read of Miguel León-Portilla's work on Tlacaelel) in this research pass.
